body.heading: The problem
paragraphs: A farmer must ferry a fox, a chicken and a bag of grain across a river. The boat holds the farmer and just one passenger at a time. Leave the fox alone with the chicken and the chicken is lunch. Leave the chicken alone with the grain and the grain is gone.

Try it on paper first: draw two banks, move one item per trip, and check both banks after every crossing. Most first attempts strand someone within three moves — which is exactly what makes the solution satisfying.

body.heading: The trick: a backwards step
paragraphs: The chicken is the troublemaker — it is both predator (of grain) and prey (of fox). So the chicken crosses first, leaving the fox safely with the inedible grain. The farmer returns alone.

Now the insight most people miss: sometimes you must bring something back. Take the fox across next — but you cannot leave it with the chicken, so the chicken rides back with you. A backwards step that feels like failure is actually the key move of the whole puzzle.

body.heading: The full crossing
paragraphs: With the chicken back on the starting bank, take the grain across and leave it with the fox — a safe pairing. Return alone one last time, collect the chicken, and cross. Everything arrives, uneaten, in seven crossings.
River puzzles like this one are centuries old, and they teach a genuinely useful habit: when a plan jams, do not just push forward. Ask what could safely move backwards to unjam it.

takeaway: Sometimes the way forward includes carrying something back — in this puzzle, the chicken rides the boat three times.
